en: Waiting in the foothills, Akshumkar
Must have known you would come this year.
From the river with sandy channels,
Akshumkar, left by your father,
Must have carried swans.
From the cliffs above the ravines
He must have carried geese.
He must have scattered his breast feathers,
Brooded for thirty-two days,
And hatched his eggs.
His offspring must have broken their shells aright.
By now his young
Must have become mottled black.
If you bring Akshumkar,
It is the time to take him.
When you arrive, his young
Will be at the pinfeather stage.
His prowess is well known to the people—
Your father, gone to Judgment,
Manas, left him as an inheritance.
That is the bird to set upon your hand,
That is the treasure left by your father Manas.
Let me describe Akshumkar:
His talons are iron, his jess plate copper;
His girth is two ells.
His eyes are black, his legs blue-speckled.
He never recoils from what he sees;
He needs no more than a bucketful of meat.
He never draws back from striving;
He needs no more than a platterful of meat.
He does not fold his tail and swoop;
He lets no swan fly from the lake.
He does not fold his wings and swoop;
Akshumkar lets no goose fly from the lake.
Bring it in a feeding bag;
Without letting his feathers grow foul,
I shall take good care of him.
Bring him to your mother!
Such is the story of Akshumkar.
Let me leave that here;
Listen once more, my son,
Let me begin with what lies beyond:
Beyond is Sary-Ozon,
Along the broad Talas;
Your father, gone to the other world,
Made that place his home.
Along that Talas
Stands your mother Kanykei's white palace,
Its doors iron and solid tin.
Though your mother was a woman,
Her splendor was considerable.
While your dear father was alive,
To your mother's fortress
No enemy made his way;
No one dared approach.
Its guards were beyond counting,
Its watchmen more numerous still.
Human noses and ears
They wore as amulets.
Before the door
There were seven jinn and spirits,
Forty swordsmen,
And sixty spearmen.
While your khan father lived,
I, your shamefaced, wretched mother,
Had so many guards.
My fortress must have fallen and faded;
The white palace where guards stood
Must have crumbled into a cattle enclosure.
All the plane trees must have been felled;
God must truly have struck it.
My orphan, its true sacred power cut off,
There is no croaking raven,
No cawing crow,
No living soul at all;
Talas must lie deserted.
Abyke and Kobosh, the six villains,
Must have fought without tiring,
Against Bakai, left by your father Manas,
And made sport of him.
Cutting off heads and spilling blood,
There must have been a terrible slaughter.
Noble Bakai, the renowned,
Has a spirit unlike any other.
Going out to exchange shots, valiant Bakai
Must have slain sixty of Abyke's men,
And become bloodstained.
With five hundred households in his charge,
Bakai must have gone and settled in a stronghold.
Building a fort where he headed,
Bakai must have blocked the road and held firm,
And gained an ill name.
Without yielding to the six villains,
Your noble uncle Bakai
Must have attained his aim.
My uncle, King Bakai's—
Unable to withstand his wrath,
Abyke and Kobosh, the six villains,
(Argyn and Kyrgyz mingled),
Kok-Zhaiyk at the head of Urbuz—
Kok-Zhaiyk must have fled in fright.
Your Talas was left deserted,
Turned into open, empty lands.
Roe deer, red deer and wild-goat kids
Must have filled its foothills.
The dry land left by your father
Must have suffered such a terrible fate.
The six villains clashed with Khan Bakai;
The reason for the turmoil,
My son, let me now tell you.
Abyke and Kobosh, the six villains,
Drew their swords and made them bloody;
Against the companion bound in life unto Judgment,
Bakai the lion, they raised a quarrel.
In the marsh of Uirulmo,
They circled round and held an assembly;
In the marsh of Chogulma,
They gathered and held an assembly.
Seeking one another, they met;
Chasing one another, they pursued.
They drove one another on,
The great assembly gathering.
Against my leopard uncle, Khan Bakai, they brought a charge;
The people of three khans reviled him.
Bringing a charge against my uncle Khan Bakai,
Turmoil among the people
Abyke the swine began.
Unable to withstand his wrath,
The many people standing there
Were nearly slaughtered outright.
'Over the sloping road of Zhorgo,
Who led her across?' they said.
'This ill-fated bitch—
Who helped her flee?' they said.
'We led her over the Ken-Kol pass;
The wretched woman who brings calamity,
We drove out of this Talas!
Over Zhorgonun-Beli's three foothills,
Who led her across?' they said.
'The lord's wife, that bitch—
Who helped her flee?' they said.
Abyke and Kobosh, the six villains,
Started the turmoil
And all the many people
They slaughtered.
Seeing this oppression,
Khan Tekechi, Khan Shygai
And Zhamgyrchy in Alkym—
The peoples of three khans gathered
And brought a charge against Khan Bakai:
'Over Zhorgonun-Beli's three foothills,
It must have been Bakai who led her;
The ill-fated, wretched woman,
It must have been Bakai who helped her flee.'
Khan Tekechi says:
'Yesterday in the afternoon,
On a moonless evening,
Wearing a blue ribbed-cloth coat,
Riding a horse such as Kok Tulpar,
His banner looming like a mountain,
Stirring the hearts of all who saw him,
His bulk half a mountain,
As though he would devour anyone he saw,
As dusk came and the sun set,
As the first of the people lay still,
A banner fluttering in his hand,
A golden-cheeked battle-axe
Gleaming at his wrist,
A man who looked like Bakai
Came rushing up.
"Who are you?" I asked, but he made no sound;
He passed by without a word,
It turned out to be Bakai himself;
He must have been taking your orphan to safety.'
Shygai stands and says:
'When dawn broke bright,
When light fell upon the earth,
In a wild cloud of dust,
Kok Tulpar beneath him,
Its mouth gaping wide,
Like a man in haste,
The white foam from its mouth
Spattering upon its breast—
I stood there half-dazed.
It turned out to be Bakai himself;
At that time, the orphan
He must have been making disappear.
Over the foothills of Uch-Koshoi,
He must have been leading her;
The wretched woman, may her house burn,
He must have been helping her flee.'
Zhamgyrchy in Alkym,
Zhamgyrchy stands and says:
'I too saw Bakai.
Yesterday evening,
A little before sunset,
In the usual afternoon hour,
I climbed a hill—and heard shouting!
It was Bakai himself,
Calling out, "Kanykei!"
On the plain Bakai was shouting,
Calling out, "Kanykei!"
Taking many skins of milk,
Taking two fat horses,
It was my uncle Bakai himself;
That calamity-bringing bitch,
He must have been seeing her away.'
Then Bakai grew angry
And spoke to the three khans:
'My three khans spurring against me,
You seized and ate my lamb nursed by two ewes!
When Manas the ocean passed away,
You said you would be my equals and my brothers!
Never leaving my poor soul in peace,
My three wandering khans,
You have eaten filth with your slander!
My precious self, as vast as Talas—
It is true that I concealed myself.
So she would not fall exhausted,
The orphan I cherished,
It is true that I helped her flee!
I hid my body, as vast as Ken-Kol;
The fierce woman bereft of good fortune,
Thinking she would perish in grief,
I thus helped her flee through Ken-Kol.
The reason I helped her flee—
Kara-Shaar and Zhambyl,
It is this same Bakai who besieged them.
Not merely the three of you, but a thousand of you,
It is this same Bakai who has beaten!'
Striking Kok Tulpar once,
Taking his battle-axe in hand,
Your uncle, your elder Bakai,
Then forced his way among them
And attacked the six villains.
When the khan died, all died,
And the common people died as well.
Fearing Bakai, the people fled;
My Talas was left deserted.
If you reach it safely, you will see,
My foal, your deserted Talas.
I shall receive many guests;
My noble son, hear me:
Let me tell many a tale.
Such are the ways of the six villains.
Let me leave this here
And begin with this side of the tale.
If you go farther on,
The waters of Talas must be overflowing,
Must have risen above the rocks.
The waters of Urbuz must have swelled;
Floods must have swept across them.
When you arrive, that Talas
Will be running in full spate.
Your earliest ancestors were all khans,
Blessed by Kyzyr from the beginning.
